analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug company monopolies on HIV/AIDS medicines with government-funded prize payments to developers.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors; a Senate subcommittee held one hearing in May 2012, and it died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away patents, marketing exclusivity, and other legal monopolies on HIV/AIDS medicines, letting any manufacturer sell the drugs. Instead of monopoly profits, companies and open-source researchers would earn prize payments from a government fund financed largely by an annual fee on health insurers, set at 0.02 percent of U.S. economic output. The goal is to pull HIV/AIDS drug prices down toward generic-competition levels while keeping money flowing to inventors.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than one million Americans living with HIV, who would see competition replace monopoly pricing on antiretroviral drugs; public and private payers who spend over $9 billion a year on these drugs; developers and open-source researchers, who would compete for prize payments; and developing countries, which would gain access to low-cost generics through a companion donor fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living with HIV and drug payers

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies anyone the exclusive right to manufacture, distribute, or sell a qualifying HIV/AIDS treatment, including patents and marketing exclusivity periods, so any company could sell the drug in competition.

In place of monopoly profits, the bill creates a Prize Fund for HIV/AIDS that pays developers based on how many patients benefit, how much a treatment improves on existing drugs, and whether they openly share knowledge and technology royalty-free.
At least 5 percent of prize payments are reserved for open-source contributors, and the bill lets multiple nonprofit intermediaries fund interim research and open sharing.
A companion Donor Innovation Prize Fund rewards companies that don't patent HIV/AIDS drugs or license them royalty-free in developing countries, so generics can compete there.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name HIV/AIDS drug makers, who would lose the exclusive rights their prices and profits rest on, and health insurers, who would pay an annual fee set so the private sector covers its share of a fund equal to 0.02 percent of U.S. GDP; that fee would likely be passed on to policyholders in premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and health insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates exclusive rights, including existing patents, for HIV/AIDS medicines outright rather than compensating patent holders, and such a taking of patent rights would almost certainly face constitutional challenge, adding years of litigation before anyone saw lower prices.

A government fund with a single director deciding what each innovation is worth could misjudge value, and replacing monopoly pricing with appropriations invites Congress to shortchange the fund in future budget fights.
The annual fee on health insurers, which scales with the share of HIV patients they cover, would likely be passed through to premiums for ordinary policyholders.

Wealth could shift between drug classes: companies that also sell HIV medicines for other diseases keep exclusivity for those uses but lose it for HIV, which could complicate investment decisions in dual-use products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with HIV, the potential upside is large: monopoly pricing on antiretrovirals would be replaced by open competition, and the bill's own findings put U.S. spending on these drugs above $9 billion a year. The real costs fall on the industry that currently captures that spending, plus a fee on insurers that lands partly on everyone's premiums. The bigger design risk is execution: converting patent incentives into a politically appropriated prize fund is untested at this scale, and a court fight over the uncompensated elimination of patents could stall or sink it. A serious idea with genuine risks, killed before any of those questions were tested.

outcome.mechanism: Bernie Sanders introduced it alone, the Senate health committee sent it to a subcommittee that held one hearing in May 2012, and the bill sat there until the Congress ended without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Prize Fund for HIV/AIDS Act in the Senate on May 26, 2011; no senator joined as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which assigned it to its Primary Health and Aging Subcommittee.
That subcommittee held a hearing on the bill in May 2012, but the full committee never voted to advance it and the Senate never took it up.
The bill died at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013 without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name HIV/AIDS drug makers kept their patent monopolies and monopoly pricing, and patients kept paying those prices. Health insurers avoided a new annual fee.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prize Fund for HIV/AIDS Act, the only sponsor; no senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee; after one May 2012 hearing, never voted the bill out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no votes and no floor action, so no partisan split is recorded; it was sponsored by a single Independent senator with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the patents and marketing exclusivity that HIV/AIDS drug prices rest on, replacing monopoly profits with prize payments. Their interest in keeping exclusivity runs directly against patients paying monopoly prices.

Insurers would owe an annual fee, scaled to their share of the health insurance market and the private sector's share of HIV treatment costs, to fund the prize pool. The fee would likely be passed into premiums, though cheaper HIV drugs would also cut insurer costs.
With exclusivity eliminated, any generic maker could sell qualifying HIV/AIDS treatments, and a companion donor fund rewards patent-free or royalty-free licensing in developing countries.
The bill reserves at least 5 percent of prize payments for open sharing of knowledge, data, and technology, and lets nonprofit intermediaries fund open research projects.
Government programs spend heavily on antiretrovirals; competitive pricing and the donor fund would lower those costs, with PEPFAR purchase savings partially recycled into the donor prize fund.
